Q: Extract data from a line graph A:

I believe you can use Python + OpenCV (cv2) to automatically strip out the noise, text, and gridlines.

  1. Color filtering (If applicable): If your data line is a different color from the grid, convert the image to HSV space (cv2.cvtColor) and use cv2.inRange() to create a mask that isolates only the line's color.

  2. To remove text or noise: Use Morphological Opening (cv2.morphologyEx with cv2.MORPH_OPEN). This applies an erosion followed by a dilation, which can literally erase thin text and small symbols while leaving your thicker graph line intact.

  3. To erase gridlines: Use the Hough Transform (cv2.HoughLinesP()) to detect perfectly straight horizontal and vertical gridlines. Once detected, you can draw over them in the background color to erase them.

  4. To patch created gaps: If removing the grid or text caused breaks in your data line, use Morphological Closing (cv2.MORPH_CLOSE) to bridge those gaps back together.

Q: Are beans created with @ConditionalOnProperty re-evaluated after Spring Boot startup? A:
  • Is @ConditionalOnProperty evaluated only during Spring Boot startup?

Yes

  • Are conditional beans re-created automatically if the property changes later?

No

  • Would another approach or design pattern be more appropriate for runtime switching between repositories?

Inject both repositories in your TreeService and use a custom mechanism to decide which one you want to use. However, right now, both repository seem to be exactly the same, with the same code. You will need to ensure each repository use the correct datasource.

Q: Is it possible with pathlib to set file modification time? A:

A long time ago I wrote a context manager class for the purpose. It's not much work.

import os

class keep_ts:
    def __init__(self, fpath):
        self.fpath = fpath
    
    def __enter__(self):
        self.stats = os.stat(self.fpath)

    def __exit__(self, type, value, traceback):
        os.utime(self.fpath, ns=(self.stats.st_atime_ns, self.stats.st_mtime_ns))
        # I'd recommend a try-except-OSError around this, with pass or other reaction

some_path = ... # possibly a pathlib.Path. os.utime() can take that, from v3.6

with keep_ts(some_path):
    pass # mess with the file.

# file times restored, except for creation time.
# even if the file system supports creation time (common on Windows),
# changing it usually requires elevated privileges and specific system APIs

Q: Linux Kernel Module - Serial Device Implementation A:

By "serial device" you apparently mean a UART device. For x86 systems that typically means a UART derived from the 8250.

Modern x86 motherboards typically no longer have any serial ports. So the interrupt used by the UART will depend on how the peripheral is connected, e.g. PCI bus.

Traditionally the UART driver interfaces with the tty subsystem as you mentioned. There is an alternate interface, the serial device bus, aka serdev, to consider.

Q: Сomma-separated sequence of declarators in C89 A:

In the code block where you state:

Is it guaranteed that a==2 and b==6

Up to C11, yes. Starting with C23, no.

Section 3.6 of C89 states the following:

A full expression is an expression that is not part of another expression. Each of the following is a full expression: an initializer; the expression in an expression statement; the controlling expression of a selection statement ( if or switch ); the controlling expression of a while or do statement; each of the three expressions of a for statement; the expression in a return statement. The end of a full expression is a sequence point.

And appendix A.2 regarding sequence points lists the following:

The end of a full expression: an initializer (3.5.7);

Which means there's a sequence point between the initialization of a and the initialization of b under C89.

The wording changed in C99 and C11. In particular, section 6.7.6p3 of C11 regarding declarators (i.e. a declaration of an object along with its initializer) states:

A full declarator is a declarator that is not part of another declarator. The end of a full declarator is a sequence point.

And appendix C regarding sequence points lists:

The end of a full declarator: declarators

So the same applies up to C11.

Starting in C23 is where things change. Specifically, the bolded passage from 6.7.6p3 above was removed as well as the line from appendix C above.

So the above guarantee no longer applies as of C23.

Note that the following passage from 6.7.9p23 of C11 / 6.7.10p24 of C23 does not apply:

The evaluations of the initialization list expressions are indeterminately sequenced with respect to one another and thus the order in which any side effects occur is unspecified

As that only applies to aggregates as per C11 6.7.9p12 / C23 6.7.10p13:

The rest of this subclause deals with initializers for objects that have aggregate or union type.
